newsitem.title: USA: Boston Beer sets direct stock buy plan.
newsitem.headline: Boston Beer sets direct stock buy plan.

text.p: Boston Beer Co, hoping to win more loyal drinkers of its Samuel Adams beer, announced Thursday a direct stock purchase plan to allow investors to buy its shares from the company and not pay brokerage fees.

"Customers are more loyal and they spend more money if they own the company," Alex Gregory, a spokesman for Boston Beer, told Reuters. "We prefer our customers would buy more Sam Adams beer with their newly available funds instead of paying commissions to brokers."

Stock buyers can join the Boston Beer plan by making an initial investment of from $500 to $10,000 or through monthly deductions of as little as $50 a month to a maximum of $10,000 from a checking or savings account.

The stock purchase plans have grown more popular with retail investors seeking a small investment in their favorite companies. Gregory said Boston Beer was encouraged to start the plan after hearing that J.C. Penney Co Inc found that its customers who joined its own stock purchase plan spent three times as much at the department stores.
The brewery hopes its beer-lovers will be as enthusiastic over the low-cost investment plan as they were when Boston Beer went public at $20 a share in Nov. 1995.

In a unique marketing move, Boston Beer offered 30,000 customers the chance to buy 33 shares for $15 each. But the craft brewer had to send back 108,000 checks when the campaign proved too successful.
And the plan just may boost Boston Beer's flat share price, which like most micro-brewers over the past year, has weakened to trade at $8.75 on Thursday.

Boston Beer, the largest craft brewer in the country, and other microbrewers have been hurt by competition in the category from new entrants from the major brewers, erratic sales and high marketing costs, analysts said.
Pyramid Breweries Inc, Redhook Ale Brewery Inc and Pete's Brewing Co all have warned of weaker earnings in recent months.

"The long-term prognosis for the craft beer business is dim at the moment," said Tom Pirko, president of consultants Bevmark LLC. "Investing in these companies is risky at best. They don't have critical mass."
However, Boston Beer, larger than its five biggest competitors in the craft beer market combined, is in a category by itself and has been growing faster than the industry rate, he said.
This week, Boston Beer claimed victory when Anheuser-Busch Cos Inc agreed to drop ads critical of the speciality brewer and its use of contract brewers around the country.
